But he said the downturn offered a chance to set about tackling issues of energy sufficiency and pollution. "We must treat this crisis, whether it lasts for a year or five years, as an opportunity to set goals for how we want to come out of it. "If we are really able to address these mega-challenges of the future then we would be able to restore the trust in leadership -- and I believe the world needs leadership." DAVOS, Switzerland (CNN) -- As the World Economic Forum kicked off in Switzerland on Wednesday, former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan declared that the global economic downturn had revealed a "crisis of global governance" that can only be solved through sweeping changes to the United Nations.

Annan believes the United Nations requires reform.

"The way we currently manage international affairs is failing and requires repair," Annan stated during the first morning of the five-day yearly gathering of political and corporate leaders from around the globe. "Significant new participants are emerging, and they must be brought into the fold and allowed to be heard."

Speaking about the U.N. Security Council, where the United States, Britain, Russia, China and France hold permanent seats and veto rights, Annan remarked: "It's impossible to keep governing the world based on nations that were victorious in a conflict six decades ago. The choice is between harmful rivalry and working together. Because we exist in an interconnected world, the sole path ahead is collaboration."

Annan serves as one of six co-chairs at this year's WEF meeting, alongside media magnate Rupert Murdoch, HSBC Chairman Stephen Green, Werner Wenning from Germany's chemical company Bayer, Indian businessman Anand G. Mahindra, and Maria Ramos, who heads the South African transport firm Transnet.

He also called on the attendees to confront three linked problems: the worldwide recession, energy and security, and climate change.

"Leaders must develop meaningful, ambitious approaches -- however extreme they might be -- that can help us achieve lasting economic expansion and provide employment for people who have lost their jobs," Annan said.

Murdoch, the News Corp. chief executive, told the delegates they must be "completely truthful about where the world stands right now," cautioning that the loss of $50 trillion in individual wealth had left people feeling "depressed and traumatized."

"Those of us in the Western world have been living far beyond what we can afford. We've enjoyed an enormous spree, and now that it's over, we must endure the correction," Murdoch said.

Yet he suggested the slump presented an opportunity to begin confronting matters of energy independence and environmental damage. "Regardless of whether this crisis endures for one year or five, we should view it as a chance to establish goals for how we wish to emerge from it. Now is the moment to craft the policies that can help resolve some of these issues."

Green, the HSBC leader, said the banking sector had to acknowledge it hadn't "covered itself in glory" in its role in the financial system's downfall, and he urged ongoing government action to "prevent a severe recession from descending into something worse."

Still, he argued that the largest banks could also be part of the solution: "I don't for a single second accept that a thriving economy is possible without thriving and properly operating international capital markets."

Wenning said he anticipated no answers coming out of this year's session, but he hoped participants might reach "a shared grasp of what caused the financial crisis," and he advocated a return to "the fundamentals of sustainable conduct."

"If we can genuinely tackle these enormous challenges ahead, then we can rebuild faith in leadership -- and I think the world is in need of leadership."

Political figures were set to enter the talks later on Wednesday, with both Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin scheduled to give speeches that would shape the agenda.

Former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan has declared that the global economic recession has exposed a profound "crisis of global governance," one that he believes can only be resolved through radical reform of the United Nations. Speaking to an audience of world leaders and business figures, Annan made the case that the current international system is ill-equipped to address the challenges of the modern era.

Central to his argument was a sharp critique of the U.N. Security Council's structure, which he characterized as outdated and no longer reflective of today's geopolitical realities. The world, Annan insisted, cannot continue to be governed based on the outcomes of a war that ended more than 60 years ago. He argued that clinging to such an antiquated framework undermines the credibility and effectiveness of the international body at a time when decisive global leadership is most needed.

Annan further emphasized that in an increasingly interdependent world, cooperation—rather than destructive competition—represents the only viable path forward. Nations, he suggested, must recognize their shared fate and work collectively if they hope to overcome the mounting challenges before them.

To this end, Annan urged delegates at the World Economic Forum to confront three interconnected challenges: the global recession, energy and security concerns, and climate change. He stressed that these issues are deeply intertwined and cannot be addressed in isolation from one another.

Adding a stark economic perspective to the discussion, news tycoon Rupert Murdoch warned that the Western world had been living far beyond its means. The consequences of this excess, he noted, had left many people feeling "depressed and traumatized," particularly in the wake of an estimated $50 trillion being wiped off personal fortunes worldwide.

# A Crisis of Global Governance: Kofi Annan's Call for Reform at Davos

Speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos, former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan delivered a pointed assessment of the international system's failings in the face of mounting global challenges. The economic recession sweeping across nations, he argued, had done more than simply devastate markets and livelihoods—it had exposed a deeper and more troubling reality: a fundamental "crisis of global governance." The institutions and structures designed to manage international affairs, Annan suggested, were no longer adequate to the demands of an increasingly interconnected and rapidly changing world.

At the heart of Annan's argument was a call for radical reform of the United Nations, with particular emphasis on the Security Council. As it currently stands, the Council reflects a geopolitical order that has long since passed. Annan pointed to the fundamental anachronism embedded in the system: the world continues to be run, in large measure, according to the interests and influence of nations that emerged victorious from a war concluded more than six decades ago. This arrangement, he warned, was simply unsustainable. The distribution of global power had shifted dramatically, yet the mechanisms of international decision-making had failed to keep pace.

Annan urged that emerging global players—the rising economic and political powers whose influence now shapes the trajectory of the world—must be integrated into these institutions. Without such integration, the legitimacy and effectiveness of international governance would continue to erode. A system that excludes those who now bear significant responsibility for global affairs cannot hope to command the cooperation necessary to address the world's most pressing problems.

Underlying this vision was a broader appeal to the spirit of collaboration over rivalry. The challenges confronting humanity, Annan emphasized, are deeply interconnected: the economic recession, the search for energy security, and the accelerating threat of climate change cannot be neatly separated or solved in isolation. These are shared crises that transcend national borders and defy unilateral solutions. In such a landscape, Annan argued, destructive competition among nations would prove self-defeating. Only through genuine international cooperation—through a willingness to work together rather than against one another—could the global community hope to meet these interlocking challenges and build a more stable and equitable future.

**DAVOS, Switzerland** — Former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan delivered a forceful appeal for sweeping reform of the world body during his remarks at the opening of the World Economic Forum, arguing that the ongoing global economic crisis has exposed deep structural weaknesses in international institutions.

Speaking before an audience of world leaders, business executives and policymakers gathered in the Swiss Alpine resort, Annan warned that the United Nations and other multilateral bodies risk becoming irrelevant unless they adapt to the realities of the 21st century.

"The architecture of our global institutions was built for a world that no longer exists," Annan told the assembly. "We cannot confront today's interconnected crises with yesterday's tools and yesterday's thinking."

"This crisis does not respect borders," he said. "It has moved from the financial centers to the factory floors, from Wall Street to the villages of the developing world, where the most vulnerable pay the highest price for mistakes they did not make."

He called on wealthy nations to resist the temptation of protectionism and to honor their commitments to development assistance, warning that abandoning the world's poorest during difficult times would carry lasting consequences.

## Reforming the Security Council

Central to Annan's remarks was a renewed push to reform the U.N. Security Council, whose permanent membership has remained largely unchanged since the organization's founding after World War II.

"A Security Council that reflects the power structures of 1945 cannot claim full legitimacy in addressing the problems of today," he said, urging greater representation for developing nations and emerging economies.

## Business and Global Responsibility

Addressing the corporate leaders present, Annan stressed that the private sector had a crucial role to play in rebuilding trust and stability. He urged businesses to embrace ethical practices and long-term thinking over short-term gains.

"The pursuit of profit and the pursuit of the common good need not be at odds," he said. "But we have seen what happens when greed goes unchecked and accountability is absent."

## A Measured Optimism

Despite the sober tone, Annan closed his address on a note of cautious hope, insisting that moments of crisis often create opportunities for meaningful change.

"History teaches us that great reforms are often born from great difficulties," he said. "Let us seize this moment not with fear, but with the courage to build institutions worthy of the challenges we face."

# World Leaders Sound Alarm at Davos 2009, Call for Global Cooperation Amid Economic Crisis

**DAVOS, Switzerland** — Against the backdrop of the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression, political and business leaders gathered at the World Economic Forum's annual meeting delivered urgent appeals for coordinated international action, warnings against protectionism, and calls to reform the institutions governing the global economy.

## A Sombre Mood in the Alps

The 2009 gathering, held under the theme "Shaping the Post-Crisis World," unfolded in a markedly subdued atmosphere compared to previous years. With banks collapsing, credit markets frozen, and unemployment rising across major economies, the customary optimism of the annual forum gave way to reflection and, in some cases, recrimination over the failures that precipitated the meltdown.

## Russia and China Take Center Stage

Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin delivered a pointed opening address, warning against excessive reliance on any single economic model or reserve currency. He cautioned that the world had grown too dependent on the United States, arguing that the crisis exposed structural flaws in the existing financial architecture. Putin urged restraint on state intervention even while acknowledging the need for government action, and he called for a more balanced global financial system.

Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao, making a notable appearance, attributed the crisis in part to "inappropriate macroeconomic policies" and an "unsustainable model of development characterized by prolonged low savings and high consumption." Without naming the United States directly, his remarks were widely interpreted as a critique of American financial practices. Wen emphasized China's commitment to maintaining growth and expressed confidence in his country's ability to weather the downturn.

## Warnings Against Protectionism

A recurring theme among speakers was the danger of retreating into economic nationalism. Numerous leaders invoked the lessons of the 1930s, warning that a wave of protectionist measures could deepen and prolong the recession.

Business figures and policymakers alike stressed that beggar-thy-neighbor trade policies would ultimately harm all parties. The specter of "financial protectionism" — banks retreating to domestic lending — drew particular concern, as leaders noted that restricted cross-border credit could starve developing economies of vital capital.

## Calls for Reforming Global Institutions

Many participants argued that the crisis had revealed the inadequacy of institutions built for an earlier era. There were widespread calls to strengthen and reform bodies such as the International Monetary Fund and to give emerging economies a greater voice in global economic governance.

The idea that the G20, rather than the traditional G7 or G8, should serve as the primary forum for coordinating international economic policy gained considerable traction, reflecting the growing weight of developing nations in the world economy.

## The Absence and Anticipation of American Leadership

The 2009 forum was notable for taking place in the early days of a new U.S. administration. With President Barack Obama having just been inaugurated, American officials kept a relatively low profile at Davos. Many attendees expressed hope that the incoming administration would embrace multilateral cooperation, while others voiced uncertainty about the direction of U.S. policy on stimulus, regulation, and international engagement.

## Business Leaders on the Defensive

Executives from the financial sector, often celebrated in past forums, found themselves defending their industry amid public anger over bailouts and bonuses. Discussions turned to the need for greater regulation, improved risk management, and a restoration of trust between the financial sector and the broader public.

Some business leaders acknowledged failures of judgment and oversight, while others cautioned that overly aggressive regulation could stifle the recovery.

## Conclusion

Davos 2009 captured a world grappling with profound economic uncertainty and searching for collective solutions. While speakers differed on causes and remedies, a broad consensus emerged around several themes: the necessity of international cooperation, the perils of protectionism, and the urgent need to modernize the institutions overseeing the global economy. Whether that consensus would translate into concerted action remained, as delegates departed the Swiss Alps, an open and pressing question.

---

# Annan Calls for Security Council Reform, Warns of Outdated Global Order

**DAVOS, Switzerland** — Former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan delivered a pointed critique of the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday, arguing that the body's structure no longer reflects the realities of a shifting global landscape and urging leaders to make room for emerging powers.

Speaking at the World Economic Forum's annual gathering in the Swiss Alpine resort, Annan said the Council's permanent membership—unchanged since the aftermath of World War II—risked undermining the institution's legitimacy at a moment when the world confronts increasingly transnational challenges.

"The Security Council must either reform itself or risk becoming increasingly irrelevant," Annan told an audience of political leaders, chief executives and civil society figures. "The geography of power has changed. Nations that were not at the table in 1945 are today driving the global economy and shaping regional security. They deserve a voice."

Annan, who led the United Nations from 1997 to 2006, pointed to rising economic and demographic heavyweights across Asia, Africa and Latin America whose absence from the Council's inner circle, he said, weakened collective decision-making on issues ranging from conflict prevention to climate change.

The current Council comprises five permanent, veto-wielding members—the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France—alongside ten rotating members elected for two-year terms. Proposals to expand the permanent tier have circulated for decades but have repeatedly stalled amid competing national interests.

## Mixed Reactions Among Co-Chairs

Annan's remarks drew a range of responses from fellow forum co-chairs, who gathered for a panel discussion on the state of global governance.

Several participants echoed his call for change. One co-chair, representing the business community, said corporations increasingly operate in a world where "power is distributed, not concentrated," and argued that international institutions must mirror that reality to remain effective.

"We cannot ask the private sector to innovate while our multilateral institutions remain frozen in another century," the executive said.

Others struck a more cautious note, warning that enlarging the Council could complicate an already difficult consensus-building process. A co-chair with a background in international diplomacy cautioned that adding permanent members—and potentially new veto powers—might deepen gridlock rather than resolve it.

"The instinct toward inclusion is right," the diplomat said. "But we must be careful that reform strengthens the Council's ability to act, rather than paralyzing it further."

A third co-chair emphasized that reform should extend beyond questions of membership to the Council's working methods, including greater transparency and constraints on the use of the veto during humanitarian crises.

## A Familiar Debate, Renewed Urgency

The discussion underscored a tension that has long shadowed debates over U.N. reform: broad agreement that the system needs updating, paired with persistent disagreement over how to achieve it.

For Annan, the stakes extend beyond institutional mechanics. He framed the reform question as central to preserving faith in multilateral cooperation itself at a time when nationalism and skepticism toward global institutions are on the rise in many parts of the world.

"Legitimacy is not a luxury," he said. "It is the foundation on which everything else rests. If people no longer believe these institutions represent them, they will look elsewhere."

Whether his appeal gains traction remains uncertain. Similar calls have been voiced at previous Davos gatherings and in the halls of the U.N. headquarters in New York without producing structural change.

Still, Annan expressed measured optimism that pressure for reform would eventually prove impossible to ignore.

"Change may come slowly," he said. "But it will come. The only question is whether we lead it, or whether it is forced upon us."

---
